==Problem==
The zeroes of the function <math>f(x)=x^2-ax+2a</math> are integers. What is the sum of the possible values of <math>a?</math>

<math> \textbf{(A)}\ 7\qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 8\qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 16\qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 17\qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 18</math>

==Solution 1==
By Vieta's Formula, <imath>a</imath> is the sum of the integral zeros of the function, and so <imath>a</imath> is integral.

Because the zeros are integral, the discriminant of the function, <imath>a^2 - 8a</imath>, is a perfect square, say <imath>k^2</imath>. Then adding 16 to both sides and completing the square yields
<cmath>(a - 4)^2 = k^2 + 16.</cmath>
Therefore <imath>(a-4)^2 - k^2 = 16</imath> and
<cmath>((a-4) - k)((a-4) + k) = 16.</cmath>
Let <imath>(a-4) - k = u</imath> and <imath>(a-4) + k = v</imath>; then, <imath>a-4 = \dfrac{u+v}{2}</imath> and so <imath>a = \dfrac{u+v}{2} + 4</imath>. Listing all possible <imath>(u, v)</imath> pairs (not counting transpositions because this does not affect (<imath>u + v</imath>)), <imath>(2, 8), (4, 4), (-2, -8), (-4, -4)</imath>, yields <imath>a = 9, 8, -1, 0</imath>. These <imath>a</imath> sum to <imath>16</imath>, so our answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) }16}</imath>.

==Solution 2==

Let <math>r_1</math> and <math>r_2</math> be the integer zeroes of the quadratic. 
By [[Vieta's Formulas]], <cmath>r_1 + r_2 = a\text{ and }r_1r_2 = 2a.</cmath>

Plugging the first equation in the second, 
<cmath>r_1r_2 = 2 (r_1 + r_2).</cmath> 

Rearranging gives 
<cmath>r_1r_2 - 2r_1 - 2r_2 = 0 \implies (r_1 - 2)(r_2 - 2) = 4.</cmath>

These factors <math>(f_1,f_2)</math> (ignoring order, because we want the sum of factors), can be <math>(1, 4), (-1, -4), (2, 2),</math> or <math>(-2, -2)</math>.

The sum of distinct <math>a = r_1 + r_2 = (f_1+2) + (f_2+2)</math>, and these factors give 
<cmath>\sum_a a = (5+4) + (-5+4) + (4+4) + (-4+4) = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }16}</cmath>.



==Solution 3==

Let the roots be <imath>r</imath> and <imath>s</imath>. By Vieta's we have that <imath>r+s = a</imath>, and <imath>rs = 2a</imath>. So by Simon's Favorite Factoring Trick: <cmath>2r+2s = rs \Longrightarrow rs-2r-2s = 0 \Longrightarrow (r-2)(s-2) = 4.</cmath> Now, we test out values of <imath>r</imath> and <imath>s</imath> to see which work. Lets say that <imath>r-2 = 1</imath>, and <imath>s-2 = 4</imath>. This implies that <imath>(r,s) = (3,6)</imath>, so <imath>a = 9</imath>. Now, we let <imath>r-2 = 2</imath>, and <imath>s-2 = 2</imath>, this gives us <imath>(r,s) = (4,4)</imath>, which gives us a value for <imath>a</imath> of <imath>8</imath>. Now, we circle an answer of <imath>17</imath> and move onto the next problem. Yikes! They didn't say that <imath>a</imath> can't be negative! This is where many people would go wrong. Let <imath>r-2 = -1</imath>, and <imath>s-2 = -4</imath>. This gives us that <imath>(r,s) = (1,-2)</imath>. This results in a value of <imath>-1</imath> for <imath>a</imath>. Now, we let <imath>r-2 = -2</imath>, and <imath>s-2 = -2</imath>. This gives <imath>a = 0</imath>. Now, we are done. Our total sum is <imath>9+8-1 = \boxed{\textbf{(C) }16}</imath>.

==Solution 4: Quadratic Formula==

We are given that the zeroes are integers. For this reason, we should use the quadratic formula on <imath>x^2 - ax + 2a</imath> to yield more information about the roots. 

After simplifying, we get that the roots are <imath>\dfrac{a \pm \sqrt{a^2 - 8a}}{2}</imath>. From this, we can see that a^2 - 8a has to be a perfect square for the roots to be integers. 

In addition, <imath>a^2 - 8a</imath> and <imath>a</imath> have to have the same parity (both even or both odd). However, that is always true (you can try out some odd/even integers)

Hence, I set up another equation: <imath>a^2 - 8a = y^2</imath>, where y is an integer.

I use the quadratic formula again for <imath>a</imath>, yielding that the roots are <imath>4 \pm \sqrt{y^2 + 16}</imath>. If we sum up 2 conjugate roots, the sum is <imath>8</imath>, so the problem boils down to finding nonnegative "Pythagorean Triples" with <imath>16</imath>. 

Hence, we get that <imath>y = 3</imath>, <imath>y = 0</imath>. Each contributes <imath>8</imath> to the running sum, so our answer is <imath>8 + 8 = 16</imath>.

Note: We can see that there are at max 2 values for <imath>y</imath>, as the answer choices indicate either <imath>8</imath> or <imath>16</imath>.
